column2: A firm identifies meaningful market segments, evaluates target attractiveness and selects a competitive position; a positioning decision does not eliminate the need to define its intended audience.
column3: Positioning consists only of dividing customers into segments and does not involve a differentiated value proposition.

column2: A large segment can be unattractive when rivalry, access cost and poor firm fit overwhelm its revenue potential; size alone is insufficient for target selection.
column3: The largest segment is necessarily the best target because competitive intensity and access costs cannot affect its profitability.

column2: Designing distinct value from competitors concerns differentiation, while grouping buyers by relevant similarities concerns segmentation; the concepts interact without being identical.
column3: Grouping buyers by income is product differentiation even if every group receives an identical offering and message.

column2: A intended position is not established solely by the firm's slogan; customer perceptions relative to alternatives determine whether the intended distinction is realised.
column3: Declaring a premium slogan establishes a premium perceptual position regardless of customers' actual associations.

column2: Three product lines with 4, 6 and 5 items give mix width 3 and total length 15; item variants affect depth rather than the number of lines.
column3: That mix has width 15 and length 3 because width counts individual items across lines.

column2: An existing brand's new flavour in the same product category is a line extension; using it for a different category is a brand extension in the stated classification.
column3: A new flavour in the existing category is necessarily a brand extension into a new category.

column2: A new item selling 1,000 units while displacing 300 equivalent old-item units generates 700 incremental units before considering contribution differences and other effects.
column3: All 1,000 new-item units are incremental company sales because the products have different labels.

column2: Observed sales growth or decline informs PLC analysis, but stage is not mechanically determined by calendar age and can be affected by repositioning or market changes.
column3: A product becomes a decline-stage product after a fixed number of years regardless of its sales and market conditions.

column2: Early screening and concept testing can eliminate weak proposals before expensive commercialisation; positive concept responses do not alone establish profitable adoption at the actual price.
column3: A favourable concept survey removes the need for business analysis or price-sensitive market testing before commercialisation.

column2: Cost Rs 80 and a 20% margin on selling price require price Rs 100; a 20% markup on cost gives Rs 96 and a different margin.
column3: A 20% sales margin and 20% cost markup both require price Rs 96 because they express the same percentage profit.

column2: Successive 20% and 10% discounts on a list price leave 72% of list price, rather than 70%, when applied multiplicatively in the stated order.
column3: Those successive discounts reduce list price by exactly 30% because discount percentages are always additive.

column2: A low introductory price may support adoption in a price-sensitive market with scale benefits, but its success still depends on costs, competitive response and later economics.
column3: Penetration pricing requires a price-insensitive market where buyers treat higher prices as the main quality signal.

column2: Skimming can recover value from early high-willingness buyers, but rapid imitation and elastic demand can limit how long a high initial price remains feasible.
column3: Rapid imitation necessarily strengthens skimming because competing substitutes reduce buyer price sensitivity.

column2: A campaign costing Rs 60,000 with incremental contribution Rs 300 per sale requires 200 genuinely additional sales to cover that campaign cost, ignoring other changes.
column3: It requires 200 total sales even if 150 of them would have occurred without the campaign.

column2: Incentives aimed at channel intermediaries illustrate a push effort; promotion inducing final-consumer demand illustrates pull, and a campaign can combine both.
column3: A distributor rebate is pull promotion solely because the distributor later sells to final consumers.

column2: A standard paid nonpersonal message and an interactive salesperson exchange have different communication characteristics; high reach does not imply equally tailored feedback.
column3: A mass advertisement gives the same individual diagnostic feedback as a personal sales conversation simply because both communicate product benefits.

column2: A short-term coupon can stimulate trial without establishing enduring brand positioning; repeated discounts can also affect reference prices and perceived value.
column3: A coupon necessarily creates a durable premium position because any rise in short-term sales proves stronger brand equity.

column2: Broad availability across many suitable outlets is intensive distribution; restricting outlets based on criteria is selective, even if selected outlets cover several regions.
column3: Selective distribution is defined solely by operating in only one geographic region rather than by outlet choice.

column2: Conflict between two retailers at the same channel level is horizontal; conflict between a manufacturer and distributor at different levels is vertical.
column3: A manufacturer-distributor conflict is horizontal because both firms participate in the same product market.

column2: Removing an intermediary does not remove the need for its logistics, assortment or information functions; another party must perform necessary functions.
column3: Selling directly eliminates every warehousing, information and delivery function previously performed by intermediaries.

column2: An aspirational reference group can influence a buyer without direct membership, while high-involvement decisions generally warrant more deliberate evaluation than habitual low-risk purchases.
column3: A reference group can influence a buyer only after formal membership and cannot affect aspirational purchases.

column2: Higher perceived risk can increase information search and reliance on trusted signals; the objective purchase price alone does not determine the buyer's perceived risk.
column3: Two equal-price products necessarily create identical perceived risk and information-search behaviour for every consumer.

column2: Doubt after a difficult choice among attractive alternatives can produce postpurchase dissonance; support can address it even when the product performs as promised.
column3: Postpurchase dissonance can occur only after a confirmed product defect and never after a satisfactory but difficult choice.

column2: Physical evidence and credible signals can reduce uncertainty about an intangible service without converting the underlying service into a storable physical product.
column3: Providing tangible brochures makes the underlying service tangible and eliminates all pre-purchase quality uncertainty.

column2: Unused appointment capacity cannot ordinarily be inventoried for later sale, so demand and capacity management address perishability rather than conventional finished-goods storage.
column3: Unused service appointments can be stored and sold next month in the same way as unsold packaged goods.

column2: Training and process controls can reduce service variability, while variation across staff, customers and timing can remain; standardisation does not logically eliminate every difference.
column3: A written service procedure eliminates all variability even when delivery involves different employees and customer participation.

column2: CRM considers retention and customer value; an expensive acquisition can be unattractive when expected contribution and retention do not recover its cost.
column3: A customer acquired at any cost is profitable whenever the first transaction generates positive revenue.

column2: Greater retention can raise lifetime value but does not guarantee it if retention concessions reduce contribution enough; the cash-flow and service-cost effects must also be assessed.
column3: Any increase in retention automatically raises lifetime value regardless of discounts, servicing costs and contribution margins.

column2: A substantiated environmental product claim differs from an unsupported green claim; social marketing seeks behaviour supporting a social objective rather than merely using social-media advertising.
column3: Every campaign posted on social media is social marketing regardless of whether it has a social-behaviour objective.

column2: Lower inventory holdings can increase stockouts or emergency transport costs; logistics optimisation considers total relevant cost and service rather than inventory cost alone.
column3: The policy with the lowest inventory holding cost necessarily minimises total logistics cost irrespective of stockouts and transport expense.
